title: Euro breaks below $1.10 as French election risk builds; three banks see $1.08 next
body: With short positioning this stretched, the euro is vulnerable to sharp short-covering rallies even if the trend stays lower. A credible French budget or a soft US inflation reading would be the likeliest triggers. On the downside, the $1.08 to $1.09 area is the next focus, where the bank forecasts and options-market risk sit. The spread between French and German bonds is the gauge to watch: if it stays contained, the move remains mainly a dollar story, and if it widens, the French element takes over. A firm dollar also keeps USD/JPY pressing against Tokyo's intervention zone near 160. --- The euro is caught between French politics and a hawkish Fed, and forecasters see $1.08 next, though positioning is now crowded enough to make the next bounce a sharp one.

title: Barclays: Back-to-back Fed hikes give the dollar staying power that a jumbo 50bp move wouldn't
body: The focus for the dollar shifts from how big the December hike will be to how long the hiking continues. That leans toward front-end Treasury yields staying high into the first quarter. It's a constructive backdrop for the dollar against lower-yielding currencies, although intervention risk near 160 limits the upside in USD/JPY. Gold faces the same headwind it has struggled with all year, as longer-lasting high US rates raise the cost of holding it. Freight and diesel costs are a direct channel from oil to US core inflation, so oil prices now feed straight into Fed pricing. --- Barclays says the dollar's strength comes from how long the Fed keeps hiking, not how big any single move is, and two quarter-point steps do that job better than one jumbo hike. Summary: Barclays forecasts 25 basis point Fed hikes in December and January, taking the target range to 4.25% to 4.50% It does not expect the 50 basis point December move Governor Waller has suggested officials should consider The bank argues two consecutive hikes would keep US rates higher for longer and support the dollar more durably than one jumbo hike October CPI rose 0.4% on the month against 0.3% expected, and Barclays sees energy, diesel and freight costs spreading into core goods prices J.P.

title: Japan's Consumer Prices Edge Higher in October, Breaking September Stall
body: Japan's consumer inflation picked up modestly in October 2026, with the Consumer Price Index (CPI, n.s.a) rising 0.8% month-over-month, according to data updated on 19 November 2026. This marks a clear shift from September 2026, when prices were flat and the index recorded 0.0% on a month-over-month basis. The latest reading indicates that price growth has resumed after a temporary pause in September, when the previous comparison period showed no change from the month before. On a month-over-month basis, October's 0.8% increase reflects renewed upward pressure in consumer prices compared with the stagnation seen in the prior month. For analysts and investors tracking Japan's inflation dynamics, the October data suggests that the disinflationary lull in September was short-lived. title: Japan's October CPI Ticks Up to 2.3% YoY, Signaling Mild Re-Acceleration in Inflation
body: Japan's national Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 2.3% year-over-year in October 2026, edging higher from September's 2.1% annual gain. The data, updated on 19 November 2026, indicate a modest re-acceleration in inflationary pressures after a slight cooling in the previous month. Both the current and previous readings are measured on a year-over-year basis, comparing price levels in each month to the same month a year earlier. September's 2.1% increase reflected conditions relative to September of the prior year, while October's 2.3% print captures the change versus October a year ago. The uptick suggests that, despite some earlier signs of easing, consumer prices in Japan continue to climb at a rate above the 2% level often watched by markets and policymakers. Investors and analysts are likely to scrutinize whether this upward move marks the start of a more sustained inflation trend or simply a minor fluctuation around the 2% zone. The October data will feed into expectations for Japan's near-term monetary policy stance and assessments of how firmly inflation is taking hold in the domestic economy. title: Japan's National Core CPI Edges Up to 2.2% in October, Extending Above-Target Inflation
body: Japan's National Core Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 2.2% year-over-year in October 2026, slightly higher than the 2.1% increase recorded in September 2026. The data, updated on 19 November 2026, underscore a continued period of inflation running above the Bank of Japan's long-standing 2% target. On a year-over-year basis, October's reading reflects price changes compared with October a year earlier, while September's figure represented a comparison with September a year earlier. The modest uptick from 2.1% to 2.2% suggests that underlying price pressures remain persistent, rather than fading, as Japan exits a prolonged era of ultra-low inflation. Investors and policymakers will be watching whether this incremental acceleration in core inflation marks the start of a more sustained trend or remains a mild overshoot. The trajectory of National Core CPI will be a key input for expectations around Japan's future monetary policy path and the yen's performance in global markets. title: Fed Reserve Balances Edge Back Above $3 Trillion, Signaling Slight Liquidity Uptick
body: Reserve balances with Federal Reserve Banks in the United States have nudged higher, returning above the $3 trillion mark, according to the latest data update on 19 November 2026. The indicator rose from $2.969 trillion previously to $3.001 trillion, marking a modest increase in bank reserves held at the Federal Reserve. The move suggests a slight easing in overall liquidity conditions within the U.S. banking system, as reserve balances reflect the funds that depository institutions hold on account at the Fed. While the change is relatively small in absolute terms, the shift back over the $3 trillion threshold will be closely watched by market participants monitoring the interplay between Federal Reserve operations, money market dynamics, and banking-system liquidity. Analysts will now be looking at subsequent readings to determine whether this uptick represents the start of a more sustained build-up in reserves or a short-term fluctuation around current levels. For the moment, the latest figure underscores that excess liquidity in the financial system remains substantial by historical standards. title: Fed's Balance Sheet Edges Lower to $6.74 Trillion, Signaling Continued Quantitative Tightening
body: The U.S. Federal Reserve's balance sheet declined slightly to $6.741 trillion, according to data updated on 19 November 2026. The latest reading marks a modest decrease from the previous level of $6.759 trillion, underscoring the central bank's ongoing effort to reduce the size of its asset holdings. The incremental drawdown in the balance sheet is consistent with a measured approach to quantitative tightening, as the Fed allows securities to mature without full reinvestment. While the move is relatively small in absolute terms, such shifts are closely monitored by investors for signals about longer-term liquidity conditions and the central bank's stance on withdrawing pandemic-era support from the financial system. title: South Korea's Producer Inflation Eases Slightly in October, PPI Slows to 7.2% YoY
body: South Korea's producer price inflation showed a modest deceleration in October 2026, signaling a slight easing of upstream price pressures in the economy. The Producer Price Index (PPI) rose 7.2% year-over-year in October, down from a 7.6% year-over-year increase recorded in September 2026. Both figures represent annual comparisons, with the October reading measuring price changes relative to October a year earlier, and the September figure comparing to the same month a year before. The data, updated on 19 November 2026, indicate that while producer prices in South Korea remain elevated on an annual basis, the gradual slowdown in the PPI could point to a tentative softening in cost pressures for businesses going forward. For markets and policymakers, the easing from 7.6% to 7.2% year-over-year may be viewed as an early sign that producer-level inflation could be past its peak, though the still-strong pace of annual increases suggests inflation risks remain present in the production side of the economy. title: South Korea's Producer Prices Slip in October, Ending Modest Inflation Streak
body: South Korea's Producer Price Index (PPI) turned negative in October 2026, signaling a mild easing of upstream price pressures. Month-over-month, the PPI fell to -0.1%, down from a 0.1% increase recorded in September 2026, according to data updated on 19 November 2026. The move marks a reversal from the previous month's modest uptick and suggests that cost pressures faced by producers have softened on a short-term basis. On a month-over-month basis, the "actual" October reading of -0.1% reflects a decline in producer prices compared with September, whereas the "previous" 0.1% figure captured the change from August to September. While the shift is relatively small in absolute terms, the transition from positive to slightly negative producer inflation may influence expectations around input costs and margins for South Korean firms, and could be watched closely for any signs of broader disinflation in the economy. title: Yield on 10-Year U.S. TIPS Climbs to 2.903%, Marking Notable Increase at Latest Auction
body: The yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) rose to 2.903% at the latest auction, up from the previous level of 2.653%. The new result, updated on 19 November 2026, reflects a notable increase of 25 basis points in the real yield on inflation-linked U.S. government debt. This move higher in the TIPS yield indicates that investors are now demanding a greater inflation-adjusted return to hold long-term U.S. government securities indexed to consumer prices. The shift may signal evolving expectations around the path of real interest rates and compensation for inflation risk over the coming decade. For markets, the higher 10-year TIPS yield is a key reference point for assessing real borrowing costs and for deriving market-based inflation expectations when compared with nominal Treasury yields. The latest auction outcome will be watched by fixed-income investors as they recalibrate portfolios in response to changing real rate dynamics in the U.S. economy. title: 2-Year T-Note futures hit 7-session high as yields slip. 11/19/26
body: 2-Year T-Note futures advanced for the third time in four sessions to reach a seven-session high of 101'305. Three factors drove the upward price action: leading economic indicators coming in below expectations, a rotation sparked by selling pressure in equity markets and pragmatic commentary from Federal Reserve officials following a more hawkish tone earlier in the week. Market pricing continues to indicate a high probability of a 25 bps rate hike at the December FOMC meeting as participants weigh recent economic data. Across the Treasury curve, yields moved lower by 1 to 3.5 bps from the 1-Year out to the 30-Year maturity. The 2-Year Treasury yield declined 3 bps to 4.77%, marking a one-and-a-half-week low, while the 10-Year yield fell 2 bps.
